title: 1 Chronicles 29:1–9
context: David tells the assembly that Solomon is young and the work is great, describes what he has prepared, and gives his own treasure of gold and silver for the house of his God. He asks who will offer willingly, and the leaders give generously, with precious stones placed in the treasury under Jehiel. The people rejoice because they offered willingly and with a perfect heart; both traditions read this as shared ground on joyful, willing giving, and the large sums and the mention of darics are discussed by interpreters.

verses.text: David the king said to all the assembly, “Solomon my son, whom alone God has chosen, is yet young and tender, and the work is great; for the palace is not for man, but for the LORD God.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Solomon my son, whom alone God has chosen, is yet young and tender, and the work is great; for the palace is not for man, but for the LORD God.” Arminian readers note David’s concern for his young son (cf. 22:5; 1 Kings 3:7).

The greatness of the work comes from the One for whom it is built.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s choice of Solomon set beside honest recognition of his youth.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: God’s choice does not remove the need for help, preparation, and the support of the assembly.

verses.text: Now I have prepared with all my might for the house of my God the gold for the things of gold, the silver for the things of silver, the bronze for the things of bronze, iron for the things of iron, and wood for the things of wood, also onyx stones, stones to be set, stones for inlaid work of various colors, all kinds of precious stones, and marble stones in abundance.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now I have prepared with all my might for the house of my God” gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and precious stones. Arminian readers note that David gave his full effort to a project he would not finish.

His preparation serves the next generation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see faithful preparation as service within God’s plan, even when another completes the work.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: faithful labor is valuable even when someone else sees its fruit.

verses.text: In addition, because I have set my affection on the house of my God, since I have a treasure of my own of gold and silver, I give it to the house of my God, over and above all that I have prepared for the holy house:
verses.arminianNotes:
David says, “because I have set my affection on the house of my God, since I have a treasure of my own of gold and silver, I give it to the house of my God.” Arminian readers note that David’s personal gift flows from love for God’s house.

He gives beyond what he had already prepared.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see generosity flowing from affection for God.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: David leads by example, giving his own treasure before calling others to give.

verses.text: even three thousand talents of gold, of the gold of Ophir, and seven thousand talents of refined silver, with which to overlay the walls of the houses;
verses.arminianNotes:
David gives “three thousand talents of gold, of the gold of Ophir, and seven thousand talents of refined silver.” Arminian readers note the generosity of the gift.

Ophir was known as a source of gold (cf. 1 Kings 9:28); the size of the figures is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a lavish gift, and leave the question of the figures’ scale to interpreters.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the gift is given to overlay the walls of the houses.

verses.text: of gold for the things of gold, and of silver for the things of silver, and for all kinds of work to be made by the hands of artisans. Who then offers willingly to consecrate himself today to the LORD?”
verses.arminianNotes:
David asks, “Who then offers willingly to consecrate himself today to the LORD?” Arminian readers note that the call is to self-dedication, not only to giving money.

The invitation is open to all.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the call to consecrate oneself, with giving as its expression.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: true giving begins with offering oneself to the LORD (cf. 2 Cor 8:5).

verses.text: Then the princes of the fathers’ households, and the princes of the tribes of Israel, and the captains of thousands and of hundreds, with the rulers over the king’s work, offered willingly;
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then the princes of the fathers” households, and the princes of the tribes of Israel, and the captains of thousands and of hundreds, with the rulers over the king’s work, offered willingly.’ Arminian readers note the leaders’ ready response.

Leaders follow the king’s example.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see willing hearts among the leaders as a blessing on the work.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the leaders’ generosity shows unity in the work of God’s house.

verses.text: and they gave for the service of God’s house of gold five thousand talents and ten thousand darics, of silver ten thousand talents, of bronze eighteen thousand talents, and of iron one hundred thousand talents.
verses.arminianNotes:
They give gold, “ten thousand darics,” silver, bronze, and iron. Arminian readers note that the daric is generally identified as a Persian coin, which many take as the Chronicler using a unit familiar in his own day.

The size of the figures is also discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the reference to darics and the large amounts, and leave these questions to interpreters.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the leaders give generously for the service of God’s house.

verses.text: People with whom precious stones were found gave them to the treasure of the LORD’s house, under the hand of Jehiel the Gershonite.
verses.arminianNotes:
“People with whom precious stones were found gave them to the treasure of the LORD’s house, under the hand of Jehiel the Gershonite.” Arminian readers note the accountability in placing the gifts under a named Levite (cf. 26:21–22).

Generosity is joined to careful stewardship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see order and trust in the handling of offerings.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: gifts for God’s work should be managed faithfully.

verses.text: Then the people rejoiced, because they offered willingly, because with a perfect heart they offered willingly to the LORD; and David the king also rejoiced with great joy.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then the people rejoiced, because they offered willingly, because with a perfect heart they offered willingly to the LORD.” Arminian readers note the joy that comes with free and willing giving (cf. 2 Cor 9:7).

David also rejoices with great joy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see willing hearts as a gift from God that produces joy (cf. 29:14).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the giving is joyful because it is willing and wholehearted, as in the tabernacle offering (Exod 35:21, 29).
